repo.description:
## Summary

An unauthenticated client can install a crafted huffman table with `DEBUG COMPRESSION SET`, store one 14 byte key, and overflow a fixed 128 byte stack buffer in `CompactObj::HashCode()` when the dash table rehashes. The shipped binary is non-PIE with no stack protector, so the overwrite gives deterministic control of the saved return address and, through a single gadget into an internal `system()` wrapper, arbitrary command execution as the Dragonfly service account. Proven end to end on the stock `ghcr.io/dragonflydb/dragonfly:v1.40.1` image in its default configuration, with ASLR enabled and no information leak.

## Severity

Critical, CVSS 3.1 base 9.8 (`AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`). Default deployments set no password and expose the `DEBUG` family on the ordinary client port.

## Affected

| | |
|---|---|
| Product | DragonflyDB |
| Version verified | v1.40.1, commit `434478e00c366c711985d0b3269023fc39db8ad1` |
| Image | `ghcr.io/dragonflydb/dragonfly:v1.40.1`, digest `sha256:ebf3c6c213e82fb51b4521660cca13f06f3421dc5b1ed14f2f474c50b5e29986`, linux/amd64 (also `latest` as of 2026-08-26) |
| Configuration | default, no authentication, no special flags |
| Class | CWE-121 stack-based buffer overflow, CWE-787 out-of-bounds write, CWE-20 |

## Root cause

`CompactObj::HashCode() const` decodes an inline huffman value into a fixed stack array with no destination bound:

```cpp
char buf[kInlineLen * 8];   // 128 bytes, on the stack
size_t decoded_len = GetStrEncoding().Decode(string_view{u_.inline_str, taglen_}, buf);
```

The safety assumption is that huffman cannot expand more than 8x, so an inline value (16 bytes maximum) cannot decode past 128 bytes. That does not hold: a huff0 table only assigns codes to the symbols it declares, so every byte outside the declared alphabet encodes in zero bits. A value made of out-of-alphabet filler compresses to almost nothing while its header declares a decoded length of about a thousand. `decoded_len` comes from attacker metadata and is never compared against `sizeof(buf)` before the write.

## Reaching the path

The member `HashCode()` runs on stored objects when the dash table rehashes, so no special command is needed after the key is stored: inserting a few thousand short keys is enough. In our runs the overflow fires at roughly 6400 filler keys.

## Exploitation

The binary is non-PIE and built without a stack protector, so both addresses are compile time constants: `base::sh_exec` (a one argument `sh -c` wrapper) at `0x004be2e0`, and the gadget `mov %r8,%rdi ; call *%rbx` at `0x011426e1`. `r8` still points at the decoded buffer when `HashCode()` returns, so the gadget sets `rdi = buf` and calls whatever the overflow placed in `rbx`:

```
ret       -> 0x011426e1   mov %r8,%rdi ; call *%rbx      (gadget, from buf+168)
rbx       =  0x004be2e0   base::sh_exec(char const*)      (from buf+136)
result    =  sh_exec(buf) = system("sh -c \"sh *\"")      (buf[0..] decodes to "sh *\0")
```

The offsets are arithmetic, not brute force. The decode of an over long inline value is exactly periodic, so a table with period 43 places the two addresses 32 bytes apart at offsets 136 and 168, exactly the frame distance, leaving the first 7 bytes free for the command string. `sh *` fits there and globs onto a snapshot staged beforehand with `CONFIG SET dbfilename x` plus `SAVE`, which `dash` executes as a script. That staging is not part of the vulnerability, only the cheapest way to expand a six character command into a full shell.

## Proof of concept

Target, published image and a port mapping only:

```sh
docker run -d --name dfpocrece -p 6331:6379 -m 2g \
  ghcr.io/dragonflydb/dragonfly:v1.40.1 --logtostderr --proactor_threads=1
```

Four unauthenticated steps: (1) install the crafted table with `DEBUG COMPRESSION SET`, (2) stage the command body (`CONFIG SET dbfilename x`, one key holding the reverse shell line, `SAVE`), (3) store the 14 byte crafted key whose header declares 1000 decoded bytes, (4) insert filler keys until the rehash calls `HashCode()`.

The listener receives a connection from the container and gets an interactive shell; `whoami` answers `dfly`. The process then dies with `SIGSEGV` (exit 139) at the instruction after `call *%rbx`, that is, where control returns once the spawned shell exits. Nothing in the run is probabilistic: no leak, no ASLR bypass, no retry loop. See `RCE-HUFFMAN.png` and the `PROOF-*` logs in this directory.

## Remediation

1. **Bound the decode destination.** The decoded size is known before a single byte is written, so `HashCode()` should reroute or refuse anything that does not fit rather than trusting a ratio:

```cpp
size_t decoded_len = enc.DecodedSize(blob);
if (decoded_len > sizeof(buf)) {
  string tmp(decoded_len, '\0');
  enc.Decode(blob, tmp.data());
  return XXH3_64bits_withSeed(tmp.data(), decoded_len, kHashSeed);
}
```

2. **Make the unsafe interface impossible to misuse.** `StrEncoding::Decode` and `HuffmanDecoder::Decode` take a bare `char*` with no capacity. Add a capacity parameter and clamp `HUF_decompress1X_usingDTable` to it, fixing the class at every call site.
3. **Validate installed tables.** `DEBUG COMPRESSION SET` should apply the coverage rule `PostProcessHist` already enforces for generated tables and reject any table that leaves a symbol without a code.
4. **Reconsider the exposure of `DEBUG`.** Letting an unauthenticated client install an arbitrary entropy coding table is a powerful primitive on its own.
repo.summary: Unauthenticated remote code execution in DragonflyDB (stack buffer overflow in `CompactObj::HashCode()`)
